title: Finding and testing rules from tables

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2; y=2,3,4. Give a simple matching rule and output at x=3.
worked_examples.answer: A matching rule is y=x+2; at x=3, y=5.
states: Output rises by one each row
At input zero, output is two
Use y=x+2 to get five at x=3

steps.title: Compare adjacent rows
steps.action: Mark plus one between both adjacent input and output rows.
steps.narration: The input and output change at the same rate.

steps.title: Find the starting value
steps.action: Circle the row at input zero.
steps.narration: Two is the constant amount added.

steps.title: Extend the rule
steps.action: Send three through add two.
steps.narration: The next output is five.

worked_examples.misconception: Copying an output without relating it to input.

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2,3; y=10,7,4,1. Give a simple matching rule.
states: Every input plus one changes output by minus three

steps.title: Follow down the table
steps.action: Record a decrease of three for each unit input increase.
steps.narration: The rate is negative three.

steps.title: Mark input zero
steps.action: Ten is the output before any input steps.
steps.narration: This is the starting value.

steps.title: Write and test
steps.action: Start at ten and subtract three x.
steps.narration: At x=3 the result is one.

worked_examples.verify: At x=0,1,2,3 the proposed rule gives 10,7,4,1.

worked_examples.q: Rule y=2x+5 has x=−2,0,2. Complete its table.

steps.title: Keep the sign
steps.action: Insert negative two inside brackets.
steps.narration: Twice negative two is negative four.

steps.title: Use zero
steps.action: The multiplier term becomes zero.
steps.narration: This reveals the starting value five.

steps.title: Use positive two
steps.action: Twice two is four, then add five.
steps.narration: Nine completes the third row.

worked_examples.repair: Keep the signed input in a visible substitution slot.

worked_examples.q: A table shows x=1→7, 2→10, 3→13. Find a simple linear rule and its output at x=0.
worked_examples.answer: A matching linear rule is y=3x+4; at zero y=4.
states: The shown rows have equal input gaps of one
Both known output gaps are three for one input step
Undo one step from x=1: 7−3=4 at x=0
A matching linear rule is y=3x+4

steps.title: Measure the step
steps.action: Compare seven and ten, then ten and thirteen.
steps.narration: Both gaps are plus three.

steps.title: Step backwards
steps.action: Subtract three from seven for the previous input zero.
steps.narration: The fixed part is four.

steps.title: Check the rule
steps.action: At x=1,2,3 formula gives 7,10,13.
steps.narration: All stated rows agree.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming the first shown output is the intercept.
worked_examples.repair: Insert the missing zero row explicitly.

worked_examples.q: Table: 0→3, 2→11, 4→19. Find a simple linear rule and output at x=3.
worked_examples.answer: A matching linear rule is y=4x+3; at x=3, y=15.
states: Inputs jump by two; outputs jump by eight
One input step changes output by four
At zero the output is three

steps.title: Compare both intervals
steps.action: Each two-input gap adds eight output units.
steps.narration: Do not mistake eight for the per-one rate.

steps.title: Divide by step width
steps.action: Eight over two gives four per one input.
steps.narration: That is the rate.

steps.title: Read the starting row
steps.action: At zero output is three.
steps.narration: Add three after four times x.

steps.title: Fill the missing row
steps.action: At three, twelve plus three is fifteen.
steps.narration: It lies between outputs eleven and nineteen.

worked_examples.misconception: Treating an eight-output jump over two input units as slope eight.
worked_examples.repair: Label both Δx and Δy arrows.

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2,3; y=0,4,8,12. Give a simple rule and explain the zero row.
worked_examples.answer: A matching rule is y=4x; zero input gives zero output.
states: Output grows by four for every unit input
At three, four times three is twelve

steps.title: Find unit groups
steps.action: One input adds four output units.
steps.narration: Each input contributes one group of four.

steps.title: Check zero
steps.action: No input groups give zero output.
steps.narration: There is no fixed extra amount.

steps.title: Name the rule
steps.action: Multiply any input by four.
steps.narration: Check all supplied rows.

worked_examples.misconception: Adding four to every input instead of multiplying by four.
worked_examples.repair: Represent input as a count of four-blocks.

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2,3; y=0,1,4,9. Find a matching square rule and output at x=4.
worked_examples.answer: A matching rule is y=x²; at x=4 output 16.
states: These are square arrays of side x

steps.title: Build square arrays
steps.action: Place a square array for each shown nonnegative x.
steps.narration: The counted cells are zero, one, four and nine.

steps.title: Read the pattern
steps.action: Each output is x multiplied by itself.
steps.narration: That gives a candidate square rule.

steps.title: Extend to four
steps.action: Count four rows of four cells.
steps.narration: The next output is sixteen.

worked_examples.misconception: Assuming every table grows by a constant output step.
worked_examples.repair: Compare square arrays and unequal differences.

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2,3; y=1,2,5,10. Suggest a simple rule and output at x=4.
worked_examples.answer: A matching rule is y=x²+1; at x=4 output 17.

steps.title: Peel off one
steps.action: Remove a single fixed tile from each displayed output.
steps.narration: The remainders are zero, one, four and nine.

steps.title: Recognise the squares
steps.action: The remainders are input squared.
steps.narration: This is not a constant-step linear rule.

steps.title: Restore the fixed tile
steps.action: Add one to each square count.
steps.narration: The candidate rule is x squared plus one.

steps.title: Extend
steps.action: Four squared plus one is seventeen.
steps.narration: Verify the given rows too.

worked_examples.misconception: Taking the changing differences as a constant rate.
worked_examples.repair: Show square blocks plus one separate fixed tile.

worked_examples.q: Only 0→0 and 2→4 are shown. Both y=2x and y=x² fit. Are they necessarily the same rule?
states: Two shown rows agree with two candidates
The rules differ on an unshown input

steps.title: Choose a fresh input
steps.action: Use one between the displayed zero and two.
steps.narration: Rows alone do not establish a unique general rule.

steps.title: Test first candidate
steps.action: Twice one is two.
steps.narration: Keep the same input for both candidates.

steps.title: Test second candidate
steps.action: One squared is one.
steps.narration: Different outputs are a counterexample.

worked_examples.verify: At x=0,2 both agree; at x=1, 2≠1.
worked_examples.misconception: Claiming a short table uniquely proves a general formula.
worked_examples.repair: Test another input or use the actual rule statement.

worked_examples.q: A plan charges R12 once plus R3 per visit. Make a table for 0,2,5 visits and give C(n).
states: One fee of twelve plus three per visit

steps.title: Separate the charges
steps.action: Show twelve once and three for each visit.
steps.narration: The fixed charge does not repeat.

steps.title: Write the formula
steps.action: Add three n to twelve.
steps.narration: n counts visits.

steps.title: Fill zero row
steps.action: With no visits only the fixed fee remains.
steps.narration: Cost is twelve rand.

steps.title: Fill two and five
steps.action: Add six or fifteen rand to the fixed fee.
steps.narration: Costs are eighteen and twenty seven.

worked_examples.misconception: Multiplying the fixed fee by visit count.
worked_examples.repair: Keep fixed and repeated charges in separate lanes.

worked_examples.q: The rule y=9−2x gives outputs at x=0,1,3. Fill the table and find y at x=5.
worked_examples.answer: Outputs at 0,1,3 are 9,7,3; at x=5, y=−1.
states: Start nine; subtract two per unit input

steps.title: Show starting value
steps.action: At zero the two x term is zero.
steps.narration: The output begins at nine.

steps.title: Use one input step
steps.action: Subtract two for x=1.
steps.narration: Output seven is lower than nine.

steps.title: Jump three units
steps.action: Three input units remove six from nine.
steps.narration: At three output is three.

steps.title: Evaluate five
steps.action: Five steps remove ten.
steps.narration: The mathematical output is negative one; no physical restriction was stated.

worked_examples.misconception: Rejecting a negative output despite no restricted context.
worked_examples.repair: Follow the signed number line through zero.

worked_examples.q: For y=4x−3, what input produces output 17? Fill rows at x=0,2 and this input.

steps.title: Set up backward row
steps.action: Write four x minus three equals seventeen.
steps.narration: The unknown is the input, not the output.

steps.title: Fill zero
steps.action: Four times zero minus three is negative three.
steps.narration: This reveals the starting row.

steps.title: Fill two
steps.action: Eight minus three is five.
steps.narration: The row is separate from the inverse task.

steps.title: Undo subtraction
steps.action: Add three to seventeen to get twenty.
steps.narration: Reverse the final flow arrow first.

steps.title: Undo multiplication
steps.action: Twenty divided by four is five.
steps.narration: Five is the input because four times five minus three equals seventeen.

worked_examples.misconception: Dividing seventeen by four before undoing minus three.
worked_examples.repair: Reverse the operation boxes right to left.

worked_examples.q: Table: x=0,1,2,3; y=0,1,4,9. A learner says y=3x. Find the first mismatch and a better matching rule.
worked_examples.answer: At x=1 the claim predicts 3 but table says 1; a matching rule is y=x².
states: Given outputs zero, one, four, nine; claim 3x
At zero, both candidate and table give zero
At one, proposed 3x gives three, table gives one
Output gaps are one, three, five
Squares of inputs match each shown row

steps.title: Do not trust the first row alone
steps.action: Zero makes many different rules appear to agree.
steps.narration: Test the next row.

steps.title: Find first mismatch
steps.action: At x=1, three x equals three, not one.
steps.narration: The proposed rule is false.

steps.title: Inspect changing gaps
steps.action: Output differences are one, then three, then five.
steps.narration: A constant rate does not fit this table.

steps.title: Test squares
steps.action: Zero, one, four, nine are the displayed squares.
steps.narration: State a matching rule without claiming uniqueness from only four rows.

worked_examples.misconception: Accepting a rule because it matches at zero.
worked_examples.repair: Check each row and name the first mismatch.

worked_examples.q: Table: 0→2, 3→11, 5→17. Assuming a linear rule, find it and fill x=2.
worked_examples.answer: The linear rule is y=3x+2; at x=2 output 8.
states: From zero to three, output rises nine
Nine divided by three is three per input
From three to five, six over two also gives three
At zero fixed part is two

steps.title: Compare first gap
steps.action: Mark three input steps and nine output steps.
steps.narration: The per-input rate is not nine.

steps.title: Confirm with another gap
steps.action: Six output units over two input units again give three.
steps.narration: Both gaps support a linear rule.

steps.title: Use zero row
steps.action: At x=0, output two is the fixed part.
steps.narration: Rule is three x plus two.

steps.title: Fill x=2
steps.action: Three times two plus two is eight.
steps.narration: Check it lies between two and eleven.

worked_examples.misconception: Dividing only one output jump by no input width.
worked_examples.repair: Draw matching input and output jump arrows.

worked_examples.q: Assume a linear rule. Table 0→4,2→10,4→16. Find the rule, output at x=−1 and input for output 22.
worked_examples.answer: The linear rule is y=3x+4; −1→1; input 6 gives 22.
states: From zero to two, output changes by six
Six over two gives rate three
At zero fixed part is four
At negative one: minus three plus four is one
For output 22: 22−4=18, divide by three gives six

steps.title: Measure both jumps
steps.action: Every two-input step adds six output units.
steps.narration: Rate is three per unit input.

steps.title: Read the zero row
steps.action: Four is the value at input zero.
steps.narration: The linear rule is three x plus four.

steps.title: Use signed substitution
steps.action: Three times negative one plus four is one.
steps.narration: Protect the negative input in brackets.

steps.title: Reverse the output
steps.action: Subtract four from twenty two to get eighteen.
steps.narration: Undo the final addition first.

steps.title: Recover input
steps.action: Eighteen divided by three gives six.
steps.narration: Run six forward and get twenty two.

worked_examples.misconception: Using the output jump six as the per-one rate.
worked_examples.repair: Label step width before calculating and verify both requested rows.

practice_questions: Table x=0,1,2 gives y=1,2,3. Give a simple fitting rule.
Each input step adds one; at zero output is one.
Table x=0,1,2 gives y=9,7,5. Give a simple fitting rule.
At zero output nine; one step subtracts two.
For y=3x+2, give outputs at x=−1,0,1.
Table 1→8,2→11,3→14. Assuming linear, find the rule and zero row.
The output rises three per input and at zero is five.
Table 0→1,2→11,4→21. Assuming linear, find the rule.
Divide output gap by input gap.
Ten over two gives five per input; at zero output one.
Table 0→0,1→6,2→12. Give a simple proportional rule.
Each input contributes six, and zero contributes zero.
Table 0→0,1→1,2→4,3→9. Give a matching square rule and output at four.
Four groups of four give sixteen.
Table 0→2,1→3,2→6,3→11. Give a simple matching rule.
The rows 0→0,3→9 fit y=3x and y=x². Show these are not the same rule.
Club fee R5 once plus R4 per visit. Give C(n) and table at n=0,2,4.
At x=0,2,3 the rule yields six, zero, minus three.
For y=5x−2, what input produces output 18?
Table 0→1,1→2,2→5,3→10. Reject y=2x+1 using the first mismatch and suggest a better matching rule.
At x=2, claim gives 5 (matches); at x=1, claim gives 3 but table says 2; y=x²+1 fits.
At one claim three differs from two; squares plus one match all rows.
Table 0→5,3→11,5→15. Assuming linear, find rule and output at x=2.
Six over three and four over two both give rate two.
Assume linear: 0→3,2→9,4→15. Find rule, output at x=−2, and input for output 24.
Divide six by two, then reverse.
mastery_questions: Table 0→4,1→6,2→8. Give a simple matching rule.
Two output units per one input; starting output four.
Table 1→9,2→13,3→17. Assuming linear, find rule and zero row.
y=4x+5; zero→5.
Four per input; step back from nine to five.
Table 0→2,2→10,4→18. Assuming linear, give rule and output at x=3.
y=4x+2; at x=3 output 14.
Eight output units over two input units gives four per input.
Table 0→1,1→2,2→5,3→10. Find a square-based rule, give output at x=4 and reject y=3x+1 at the first mismatch.
y=x²+1; at x=4 output 17; y=3x+1 fails at x=1, predicting 4 rather than 2.
Subtract one and recognise squares; test first positive input.
Assuming linear, table 0→6,2→12,4→18. Find rule, output at −1, input for output 27, and check all given rows.
y=3x+6; −1→3; output 27 comes from input 7; rows 6,12,18 agree.
Rate six over two is three; subtract six and divide three to reverse 27.
reassessment_questions: Table 0→7,1→9,2→11. Give a simple fitting rule.
Two per input and starting value seven.
Assuming linear: table 0→1,3→10,5→16. Find rule and output at x=2.
Nine over three and six over two give rate three.
For y=4x−5, find output at x=−1 and input for output 15.
4(−1)−5=−9; undo minus five then multiply four: (15+5)÷4=5.
